Live from NPR News, I'm Charles Snyder. President Trump was in Kansas last night
making a campaign stop near Wichita two weeks before the midterm election.
He held a rally to support Republican Senator Roger Marshall
as Meg Britton-Mellish of member station KMUW reports.
Kansas Republicans joined Trump with a message for conservative voters.
Even in deep red Kansas, the midterm races are too close to stay home.
The president lent his support to the governor's race
but made clear that his focus was on re-electing Marshall.
And Roger Marshall is all that stands between the people of Kansas
and communists controlling the United States Senate
because if they get a couple of these people in, they're going to have total control.
Marshall is a staunch Trump loyalist and is currently neck and neck
with Democrat and Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton.
If Democrats pick up four seats in November,
they have a majority in the Senate.
For NPR News, I'm Meg Britton-Mellish in Wichita, Kansas.
President Trump also warned against electing Democrats
saying they want to make the U.S. more like France,
which has experienced days of rioting.
Overnight curfews have been put in place in parts of France
and Parris Eleanor Beardsley reports that the French prime minister
gave local authorities curfew power to counter what he calls delinquents and thugs.
The curfew includes Parris's Place de la République, a central gathering point
that has seen some of the worst skirmishes between protesters and police,
as well as disruption and looting.
The mayor of Nice announced a curfew specifically for young people.
There are also restrictions in some northern cities,
including Lille, which saw its town hall broken into over the weekend.
President Emmanuel Macron and his government are being blamed for the mayhem.
Far right leader Marine Le Pen said the interior minister was not prepared and should resign.
The prime minister says ultra-left radical groups are trying to create chaos
ahead of the next presidential election.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Paris.
South Korea threatened decisive retaliation
to any military provocations by North Korea following a spike in tensions.
NPR's Anthony Kuhn reports from Seoul.
The South's Joint Chiefs of Staff says it instructed troops
along the Demilitarized Zone, or DMZ,
to respond decisively to any incursions by North Korean troops.
On Monday, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un's sister Kim Yo-jong
accused the South of broadcasting warnings and firing warning shots at the North.
She said Pyongyang is considering resuming propaganda broadcasts,
which were suspended last year, and deploying more weapons along the DMZ.
Tensions have surged following a landmine blast in the DMZ last month,
which injured three South Korean soldiers.
There's been speculation that President Trump
could meet with Kim Jong-un during a summit in China next month.
But Trump told reporters he's unsure if anyone is requesting such a meeting.
Anthony Kuhn, NPR News, Seoul.
And you're listening to NPR News.
Trump administration is escalating its fight with California
over that state's voter rolls.
The Justice Department has charged 28 green card holders
for registering to vote or voting illegally.
California's Democratic Attorney General Rob Bonta
says the arrests are, in his words, "a drop in the bucket."
California has more than 23 million registered voters.
The state of Florida has secured an arrest warrant
for former Cuban leader Raul Castro.
Castro is charged with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder
in connection with the 1996 shoot-down of two unarmed U.S. planes
that were on a humanitarian mission.
Regan McCarthy, member of station WFSU, reports.
The planes were part of a group called Brothers to the Rescue.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeyer says the death of four men aboard
was not an accident.
He says evidence points to an alleged conspiracy
that involved spies within the organization
as well as government offices.
They reported on plans, logistics, and flights.
They gave information to the communist tyrants
that ultimately called in the order.
Raul Castro called for the planes to be shot down.
He called for murder.
Uthmeyer says Castro, who's now 95, won't face immediate consequences,
but he says it will impact Castro's ability to travel,
for example, to seek health care.
For NPR News, I'm Regan McCarthy in Tallahassee.
Asian shares are retreating mostly lower in Tuesday trading
after artificial intelligence stocks bounce back on Wall Street.
I'm Giles Snyder.
This is NPR News.
